title: Memento pattern
idea: The Memento pattern lets an object save its state into an opaque snapshot and later restore it, so undo works without exposing the object's internals.
points: The originator creates snapshots (mementos) of its own state and restores from them.
The caretaker stores snapshots it cannot read; only the originator opens them.
Snapshots must copy mutable state, or later edits rewrite the saved past.
For huge state, store small inverse commands instead (the Command pattern, c08).

steps.caption: The editor starts empty. The history holds nothing yet.
`checkpoint()` asks the editor for a snapshot and pushes it. Then `a` is typed.
Before `b`, another snapshot. It is a copy, so typing `b` cannot change it.
Before `c`, a third snapshot. Capacity is 2, so the oldest is dropped.
`undo()` pops the newest snapshot and hands it back to the editor to restore.
A second undo restores `[a]`. The history is now empty.
With nothing left, `undo()` returns false. The empty state was lost to the capacity limit.

code.title: The problem: aliased getters
code.caption: The caller saves state through getters. It saves a reference, not a copy, so undo does nothing.

walk.text: Getters and setters exist only for saving. Every field is now public in all but name.
The caller must know which fields make up the state. Add a field and undo misses it.
`getLines` returns the live list. The saved value and the editor share one object.
Typing mutates that shared list, so the 'saved' lines change too.
Undo restores the same two lines with cursor 1: the state is now inconsistent.

code.title: The fix: opaque snapshots
code.caption: The editor makes and reads its own snapshots. The history only stacks them, up to a limit.

walk.text: Private fields and a private constructor: only `Editor` can build or read a snapshot.
`List.copyOf` takes an immutable copy, so later typing cannot rewrite history.
Save and restore live in the originator. Add a field and only this class changes.
The caretaker holds `Editor.Snapshot` values but has no way to look inside them.
A capacity bound stops unlimited growth; the oldest snapshot is dropped first.
Undo on an empty history returns false instead of throwing.
Checkpoint before each change, so each undo returns to the state before it.

pitfalls: Storing a mutable list in a snapshot without copying makes undo restore today's state, not yesterday's.
A `record` snapshot exposes its fields through accessors; the caretaker can read and depend on them.
An unbounded undo stack of full snapshots grows memory with every keystroke; cap it or diff.

quiz.why: A record stores the reference it is given. It does not copy, so the snapshot and `live` share one list; copy in the constructor.

takeaway: Snapshot by copy, keep it opaque, and let only the originator restore.
